findings.what: Mutation runs cover 13 of 33 src files (parser, lexer, budget, dedup, rank/mod, bm25, boost, tokens, text_search, pipeline, ts/parse, agent, cli). Skipped: analysis/ts/mod.rs, registry, file_analysis, query/plan.rs, rank/tokenize_doc.rs, types.rs, error.rs, digest.rs, file_io.rs, output.rs, main.rs. The justfile recipe is `cargo mutants --workspace` (all files, default timeout, default jobs). A '92% caught' figure from the per-file runs is not the figure the justfile recipe would produce.
findings.evidence: Tallied from mutants-*/mutants.out/outcomes.json: caught 382, missed 34, timeout 33, unviable 34. 382/(382+34)=91.8%, which matches 92% only if timeouts are dropped from the denominator. Counting timeouts as not caught gives 382/449=85%. Counting them as caught gives 415/449=92.4%, so the timeout treatment decides the number. Unviable is excluded in all cases.
findings.fix: Publish caught/missed/timeout/unviable separately with the file list, or run the justfile recipe unchanged and report that.

findings.quote: TIMEOUT  crates/monokl/src/query/lexer.rs:31:9: replace Lexer<'a>::peek -> Option<char> with Some(Default::default()) in 1s build + 60s test
findings.what: 21 of 31 lexer mutants and 12 of 161 ts/parse.rs mutants end in TIMEOUT because the mutated code loops forever. They are reported neither as caught nor as missed. The 60 s timeout is about 15x the 4 s baseline test time, so each run spends the full 60 s waiting. Hung tests are only an implicit kill, not a assertion failing on behavior.
findings.evidence: log-lexer.txt shows TIMEOUT lines for 21 mutants; log-tsparse.txt shows baseline '12s build + 4s test'. Lexer has 9 caught, 0 missed, 21 timeouts, so its per-file rate is 100% or 30% depending on timeout treatment.
findings.fix: Report timeouts as their own row; use --timeout-multiplier 5 or similar so hangs cost seconds; state that a hang is a kill, not a behavioural assertion.

findings.what: The 'maxrss_kb(cum)' number is the maximum RSS over ALL children the Python process has waited on so far, not the RSS of this one run. The `before` value read on line 9 is never subtracted or printed. On macOS ru_maxrss is in bytes, not KB, so the label 'kb' is wrong by 1024x. A figure like '335 MB for a 40 MB file' therefore depends on the order of the cases (the 40 MB case runs after deep JSX and the other nesting cases and before the 20k case), and is a high-water mark across earlier cases, not per-file memory.
findings.evidence: Read run.py in full. The 40MB case writes 'a'*40_000_000 in one line; the file on disk is 38.1M. 335 MB/38.1 MB is about 8.8x only if no earlier case set the high-water mark.
findings.fix: Run each case in a fresh Python process, or use `/usr/bin/time -l` per command; label the unit as bytes on darwin.

findings.what: Stress and timing use a release binary built in the first-release worktree, not the fix-entire-pr checkout that mutation testing and the review target. Numbers (7.4 s for 20k files, 335 MB) describe a different commit than the one being reviewed. Release uses lto=true. A consumer who installs from crates.io/Homebrew gets a release build, so release is right, but its commit must be named.
findings.evidence: BIN path in run.py and run2.py; Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true. I did not diff the two worktrees' sources.
findings.fix: Print `monokl --version` and the git SHA in the harness header; rebuild from the reviewed commit before publishing numbers.

findings.quote:
for i in range(20000):
    open(os.path.join(d, f"f{i}.ts"), "w").write(f"export function needle{i}() {{ return {i}; }}\n")
findings.what: The '20k files' fixture is 20,000 identical 40-byte one-function files in a single flat directory, with no imports, no subdirectories, no .gitignore or node_modules, and every file matching the query. It is a ceiling test, not a realistic repo. Timing is one sample, from a single `search needle`, with a freshly generated tree: the files were just written (warm OS page cache), and the monokl cache state is not controlled (the first run on a fresh dir is cold, with no repeat). So 7.4 s is a single cold run on an unrepresentative corpus, and every file matching means ranking and dedup work on 20k hits. The known O(n^2) dedup is likely what dominates, not 'file count'.
findings.evidence: Read run.py section 5 in full; timing is `time.time()` around subprocess.run including Python process spawn and capture_output pipe drain.
findings.fix: Time cold and warm separately with N>=5 runs, using a real checked-out TS repo plus this synthetic as the stress case; state which.

findings.quote: p = subprocess.run([BIN] + args, cwd=ROOT, capture_output=True, timeout=timeout)
findings.what: Invocation differs from the agent call: it passes an absolute scan dir as the 2nd arg with cwd set to a parent that holds 28 other fixture dirs. A consumer runs `monokl search <query>` from the repo root with no path. Output is truncated to 160 chars, so output size and the token budget path are never exercised. No result cap flags or budget flags are passed, and stderr is cut to 160 chars so diagnostics are never examined.
findings.evidence: run.py lines 9-13; no --budget or similar flag is used in any invocation. Not verified against the CLI, since the CLI flags were not enumerated here.
findings.fix: Add cases that run without a path from the project root, and record full stdout byte counts.

findings.what: The harness never asserts anything. It prints exit codes and 160-char slices, so 'passed' means 'did not crash or time out'. Correctness cases (guard bypass, encodings, overload) are only eyeballed, and the 'ok' label is judgement after the fact. A stress run that says 'no stack overflow' is a statement about exit status only.
findings.evidence: Read run.py and run2.py in full: no assert, no expected output table.
findings.fix: Add expected exit codes and expected substring per case, and fail the script on mismatch.

findings.what: Eval directories eval-panda, eval-caliper, eval-pages are missing, so the 36-task eval (6.4x tokens, 34/36 vs 20/36 hits) could not be audited: no tasks.md, truth.md, out-*.txt, rg-*.txt, mk_*.txt or scripts exist to check how rg was invoked, who ran it, or whether ground truth was frozen first. Matching files elsewhere in /tmp/claude-501 (ac88-*.txt, hits.txt, h2.txt, idx_hits.txt) are from other projects (caliper/oracle code), not this eval.
findings.evidence: ls: eval-caliper, eval-panda, eval-pages: No such file or directory. The repo (README, ARCHITECTURE, docs/research) contains none of 6.4x, 34/36, 20/36, 7.4 s, 335 MB or 92%, so the figures are unpublished in-tree and cannot be traced to a harness.
findings.fix: Restore or re-generate the eval directories and commit the task list, truth file and driver script; until then do not publish 6.4x or 34/36.

findings.what: Without the files I cannot state the harness configuration. These questions decide whether the numbers would change, so treat the headline claims as unverified: (a) tokens estimated as bytes/4 rather than a real tokenizer; code, paths and TOON punctuation tokenize differently from prose, so a 6.4x ratio can shift in either direction; (b) whether rg was run by the person who knew the answers; (c) hit count scored with truth fixed before the run; (d) one sample per task, so 34/36 vs 20/36 has a wide interval (about +-15 points at n=36); (e) whether rg got output caps, -C context or file filters an agent would use.
findings.evidence: grep-only on absent files; this entry lists open questions, not observed facts.
findings.fix: Write the harness config in the report: binary and commit, cwd, flags for both tools, cap, tokenizer, who ran it, truth freeze time, samples.

findings.what: The CI coverage gate uses nextest with --all-features, while the user-facing `just test` runs both an all-features and a default-features pass. The 90% gate is therefore measured on all-features only. Code that compiles only in default features is not covered by the gate, which is the gap the test recipe comment says it closes. The mutation run uses `--features default`, a third configuration. Three harnesses, three feature sets.
findings.evidence: justfile coverage and test recipes; run.sh --features default.
findings.fix: Align the feature set across coverage, mutants and test, or state which one the 90% and 92% refer to.

findings.what: Stack-depth stress runs on a release binary with the OS main-thread stack and a nesting synthesized with a single construct. Real consumers run the default build too and could call from a thread pool of the Wisp embedder (library use) with a smaller stack (2 MiB for spawned Rust threads vs 8 MiB main). A pass on the main thread does not show the guard works for the library path.
findings.evidence: Not verified: I did not read how the pipeline spawns threads (grep-only).
findings.fix: Run the deep-nesting cases through the library API on a thread with the default 2 MiB stack.

Skipped: analysis/ts/mod.rs, registry, file_analysis, query/plan.rs, rank/tokenize_doc.rs, types.rs, error.rs, digest.rs, file_io.rs, output.rs, main.rs. The justfile recipe is `cargo mutants --workspace` (all files, default timeout, default jobs). A '92% caught' figure from the per-file runs is not the figure the justfile recipe would produce.
findings.evidence: Tallied from mutants-*/mutants.out/outcomes.json: caught 382, missed 34, timeout 33, unviable 34. 382/(382+34)=91.8%, which matches 92% only if timeouts are dropped from the denominator. Counting timeouts as not caught gives 382/449=85%. Counting them as caught gives 415/449=92.4%, so the timeout treatment decides the number. Unviable is excluded in all cases.
findings.fix: Publish caught/missed/timeout/unviable separately with the file list, or run the justfile recipe unchanged and report that.

findings.quote: TIMEOUT  crates/monokl/src/query/lexer.rs:31:9: replace Lexer<'a>::peek -> Option<char> with Some(Default::default()) in 1s build + 60s test
findings.what: 21 of 31 lexer mutants and 12 of 161 ts/parse.rs mutants end in TIMEOUT because the mutated code loops forever. They are reported neither as caught nor as missed. The 60 s timeout is about 15x the 4 s baseline test time, so each run spends the full 60 s waiting. Hung tests are only an implicit kill, not a assertion failing on behavior.
findings.evidence: log-lexer.txt shows TIMEOUT lines for 21 mutants; log-tsparse.txt shows baseline '12s build + 4s test'. Lexer has 9 caught, 0 missed, 21 timeouts, so its per-file rate is 100% or 30% depending on timeout treatment.
findings.fix: Report timeouts as their own row; use --timeout-multiplier 5 or similar so hangs cost seconds; state that a hang is a kill, not a behavioural assertion.

findings.what: The 'maxrss_kb(cum)' number is the maximum RSS over ALL children the Python process has waited on so far, not the RSS of this one run. The `before` value read on line 9 is never subtracted or printed. On macOS ru_maxrss is in bytes, not KB, so the label 'kb' is wrong by 1024x. A figure like '335 MB for a 40 MB file' therefore depends on the order of the cases (the 40 MB case runs after deep JSX and the other nesting cases and before the 20k case), and is a high-water mark across earlier cases, not per-file memory.
findings.evidence: Read run.py in full. The 40MB case writes 'a'*40_000_000 in one line; the file on disk is 38.1M. 335 MB/38.1 MB is about 8.8x only if no earlier case set the high-water mark.
findings.fix: Run each case in a fresh Python process, or use `/usr/bin/time -l` per command; label the unit as bytes on darwin.

findings.what: Stress and timing use a release binary built in the first-release worktree, not the fix-entire-pr checkout that mutation testing and the review target. Numbers (7.4 s for 20k files, 335 MB) describe a different commit than the one being reviewed. Release uses lto=true. A consumer who installs from crates.io/Homebrew gets a release build, so release is right, but its commit must be named.
findings.evidence: BIN path in run.py and run2.py; Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true. I did not diff the two worktrees' sources.
findings.fix: Print `monokl --version` and the git SHA in the harness header; rebuild from the reviewed commit before publishing numbers.

findings.quote:
for i in range(20000):
    open(os.path.join(d, f"f{i}.ts"), "w").write(f"export function needle{i}() {{ return {i}; }}\n")
findings.what: The '20k files' fixture is 20,000 identical 40-byte one-function files in a single flat directory, with no imports, no subdirectories, no .gitignore or node_modules, and every file matching the query. It is a ceiling test, not a realistic repo. Timing is one sample, from a single `search needle`, with a freshly generated tree: the files were just written (warm OS page cache), and the monokl cache state is not controlled (the first run on a fresh dir is cold, with no repeat). So 7.4 s is a single cold run on an unrepresentative corpus, and every file matching means ranking and dedup work on 20k hits. The known O(n^2) dedup is likely what dominates, not 'file count'.
findings.evidence: Read run.py section 5 in full; timing is `time.time()` around subprocess.run including Python process spawn and capture_output pipe drain.
findings.fix: Time cold and warm separately with N>=5 runs, using a real checked-out TS repo plus this synthetic as the stress case; state which.

findings.quote: p = subprocess.run([BIN] + args, cwd=ROOT, capture_output=True, timeout=timeout)
findings.what: Invocation differs from the agent call: it passes an absolute scan dir as the 2nd arg with cwd set to a parent that holds 28 other fixture dirs. A consumer runs `monokl search <query>` from the repo root with no path. Output is truncated to 160 chars, so output size and the token budget path are never exercised. No result cap flags or budget flags are passed, and stderr is cut to 160 chars so diagnostics are never examined.
findings.evidence: run.py lines 9-13; no --budget or similar flag is used in any invocation. Not verified against the CLI, since the CLI flags were not enumerated here.
findings.fix: Add cases that run without a path from the project root, and record full stdout byte counts.

findings.what: The harness never asserts anything. It prints exit codes and 160-char slices, so 'passed' means 'did not crash or time out'. Correctness cases (guard bypass, encodings, overload) are only eyeballed, and the 'ok' label is judgement after the fact. A stress run that says 'no stack overflow' is a statement about exit status only.
findings.evidence: Read run.py and run2.py in full: no assert, no expected output table.
findings.fix: Add expected exit codes and expected substring per case, and fail the script on mismatch.

findings.what: Without the files I cannot state the harness configuration. These questions decide whether the numbers would change, so treat the headline claims as unverified: (a) tokens estimated as bytes/4 rather than a real tokenizer; code, paths and TOON punctuation tokenize differently from prose, so a 6.4x ratio can shift in either direction; (b) whether rg was run by the person who knew the answers; (c) hit count scored with truth fixed before the run; (d) one sample per task, so 34/36 vs 20/36 has a wide interval (about +-15 points at n=36); (e) whether rg got output caps, -C context or file filters an agent would use.
findings.evidence: grep-only on absent files; this entry lists open questions, not observed facts.
findings.fix: Write the harness config in the report: binary and commit, cwd, flags for both tools, cap, tokenizer, who ran it, truth freeze time, samples.

findings.what: The CI coverage gate uses nextest with --all-features, while the user-facing `just test` runs both an all-features and a default-features pass. The 90% gate is therefore measured on all-features only. Code that compiles only in default features is not covered by the gate, which is the gap the test recipe comment says it closes. The mutation run uses `--features default`, a third configuration. Three harnesses, three feature sets.
findings.evidence: justfile coverage and test recipes; run.sh --features default.
findings.fix: Align the feature set across coverage, mutants and test, or state which one the 90% and 92% refer to.

findings.what: Stack-depth stress runs on a release binary with the OS main-thread stack and a nesting synthesized with a single construct. Real consumers run the default build too and could call from a thread pool of the Wisp embedder (library use) with a smaller stack (2 MiB for spawned Rust threads vs 8 MiB main). A pass on the main thread does not show the guard works for the library path.
findings.evidence: Not verified: I did not read how the pipeline spawns threads (grep-only).
findings.fix: Run the deep-nesting cases through the library API on a thread with the default 2 MiB stack.
